content: The guidelines for managing sexually transmitted infections (STIs) must be updated to reflect the evolving landscape of diagnostic and treatment options. This includes revising the syndromic management algorithm for genital ulcer disease (GUD) and re-evaluating other syndromes, such as vaginal discharge. Additionally, there is an urgent need to address syndromic management for specific populations, such as men who have sex with men (MSM) and sex workers, particularly for anorectal infections, as many of these cases remain undiagnosed and untreated in the absence of clear guidelines. The advent of rapid point-of-care diagnostic tests (POCTs) is transforming STI management. For example, rapid syphilis tests are now widely available, enabling broader screening and earlier treatment initiation for those who test positive. Efforts are ongoing to develop POCTs for other STIs, which will enhance the syndromic management of symptomatic cases and improve the detection of asymptomatic infections. Updated guidelines are needed to integrate these rapid tests into syndromic management protocols and provide clear algorithms for testing and screening. Despite advancements in diagnostics, therapeutics, vaccines, and barrier methods, access to these technologies remains limited, particularly in regions with the highest burden of STIs. To maximize their impact, global STI management guidelines must include strategies tailored to settings with limited access to modern technologies, as well as those where such technologies are available. Countries are strongly encouraged to adapt updated global guidance into standardized national protocols, taking into account local epidemiological data and antimicrobial resistance patterns. National guidelines for effective STI management should be developed in close collaboration with local experts in STIs, public health, and laboratory sciences. The World Health Organization (WHO) has proposed a phased approach to revising STI guidelines, addressing a range of infections and issues. Phase 1 focuses on treatment recommendations for specific STIs, including chlamydia, gonorrhea, genital herpes, and syphilis, as well as syphilis screening and treatment for pregnant women. Phase 2 emphasizes STI prevention strategies, such as condom use, behavior change communication, biomedical interventions, and vaccines. Phase 3 addresses the treatment of additional infections, such as trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis, chancroid, donovanosis, human papillomavirus (HPV), scabies, and pubic lice. Phase 4 provides guidance on laboratory diagnosis and screening. Syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum, is a significant STI associated with high morbidity and mortality. Mother-to-child transmission of syphilis (congenital syphilis) can have devastating consequences for the fetus if maternal infection is not detected and treated early in pregnancy. In 2012, syphilis was estimated to cause 350,000 adverse pregnancy outcomes globally, including 143,000 stillbirths, 62,000 neonatal deaths, 44,000 preterm or low-birth-weight infants, and 102,000 infected infants. Early screening and treatment of pregnant women can prevent these outcomes, and global efforts to screen and treat syphilis in pregnancy are beginning to show a decline in mother-to-child transmission rates. Laboratory diagnosis of syphilis involves a combination of patient history, physical examination, and testing. Many individuals with syphilis are asymptomatic or have mild symptoms, making screening essential, particularly for pregnant women. Serological tests for syphilis are divided into non-treponemal and treponemal tests. A presumptive diagnosis requires a positive result from at least one test type, while a confirmed diagnosis requires positive results from both. Rapid syphilis tests (RSTs) have been developed to detect treponemal antibodies within 10–15 minutes and can be performed in any setting without the need for refrigeration or specialized equipment. However, these tests do not distinguish between active and previously treated infections. The WHO emphasizes the importance of early syphilis screening and treatment during pregnancy, ideally before the second trimester, to prevent fetal complications. Screening all pregnant women at their first antenatal visit is recommended and is being scaled up in many countries committed to eliminating mother-to-child transmission of syphilis and HIV. The WHO guideline development process involves systematic reviews of evidence, including diagnostic test accuracy, treatment outcomes, and cost-effectiveness analyses. Recommendations are based on the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, which assesses the quality of evidence at four levels: high, moderate, low, and very low. The guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for syphilis screening and treatment in pregnant women, supporting countries in updating their national protocols to prevent mother-to-child transmission of syphilis.
